exclude: BASIC II's workspace: the integer variables, the variables' catalogue, its stacks and its buffers
the MOS's sound workspace and buffers, the printer buffer and envelopes 1-4
the MOS's definitions of the function keys
the DFS's NMI routine, the extended vectors and the paged ROMs' workspace bytes
the DFS's workspace: the catalogue and the file buffers
above the program: BASIC's variables, what earlier programs left in memory, and the screen
the rest of the zero page BASIC leaves to programs, which nothing in this part uses

comments.text: Set to 0 by every routine of the machine code before it prints, as is &71; nothing in either adventure reads it. BASIC leaves &70-&8F to the program.
Set to 0 with &70 by every routine of the machine code; nothing reads it either.

CALL &900, from FNCity: the upper part of the City's ruin. Each of these routines is the same: it zeroes &70 and &71, which nothing reads, and prints its table, one byte at a time through OSWRCH, the X register counting; the table holds VDU codes, TAB moves (31,x,y) and teletext characters, so the routine is a faster PRINT. This one's BEQ lands on &0994, the next routine, so a CALL &900 draws that one's table too.

&900's table, 127 bytes: rows 2 to 12 at column 9, the left side of the ruin in magenta graphics (the colour PROCb put at column 7), rising to a broken top at row 2, with green cracks on magenta new-background bands from row 8 down; it ends with VDU 30, cursor home.
CALL &994, from FNCity, and after &900's table: prints the 18 bytes at &09A9.
&994's table, 18 bytes: row 12 from column 19, a broken stretch of the ruin's middle; the RTS after it ends the routine. FNCity calls &994 after &900, so it is drawn twice.
RTS: the end of &994's routine, and of &900's, which runs on into it.
CALL &9BC, from FNLake: prints the 127 bytes at &09D1.

&9BC's table, 127 bytes: rows 12 to 16 of the lake in the window &A81 sets, columns counted from 2: the blue water, green islands, red twigs in the water, and magenta water plants with white tips; the RTS after it ends the routine.
RTS: the end of &9BC's routine, the lake's middle.
CALL &A51, from FNLake: prints the 26 bytes at &0A66.
&A51's table, 26 bytes: a graphics character and a new background at the cursor where &9BC left it, then row 17, the lake's lower shore in blue and magenta; the RTS after it ends the routine.
RTS: the end of &A51's routine, the lake's lower shore.
CALL &A81, from FNLake: prints the 57 bytes at &0A96.

&A81's table, 57 bytes: VDU 28,2,24,39,0, a text window from column 2 that &9BC and &A51 then draw in, and rows 10 and 11, the far shore of the lake, its top edge in blue against the yellow and green; the RTS after it ends the routine.
RTS: the end of &A81's routine, the lake's far shore and its window.
CALL &AD0, from PROCw: prints the 26 bytes at &0AE5.
&AD0's table, 26 bytes: TAB(8,1), `WEATHER REPORT` in white on a red band (codes &81, &9D, &87, then &9C), and TAB(0,5), in PROCk's window; the RTS after it, the file's last byte, ends the routine.
RTS: the end of &AD0's routine, the weather report's title, and the last byte of CODE1/1.
CALL &C00, from FNCity: prints the 125 bytes at &0C15.
&C00's table, 125 bytes: rows 13 to 17 from column 9, the lower part of the ruin in magenta with green cracks and black gaps; the RTS after it ends the routine.
RTS: the end of &C00's routine, the ruin's lower part.
CALL &C93, from FNCity: prints the 24 bytes at &0CA8.
&C93's table, 24 bytes: row 18 from column 13, the base of the ruin, which line 10630 carries on to row 21; the RTS after it ends the routine.
RTS: the end of &C93's routine, the ruin's foot.
CALL &CC1, from FNMountains: prints the 24 bytes at &0CD6.
&CC1's table, 24 bytes: the Bird of Doom in red graphics on rows 1 and 2 from column 15, its wings spread over its body; the RTS after it, the file's last byte (&0CEE), ends the routine.
RTS: the end of &CC1's routine, the Bird of Doom, and the last byte of CODE1/2.

Lines 1-2. The program arrives at &1900, PAGE on a machine with a disc interface, and line 1 sends it to lines 32220-32225, which copy it to &0E00 and RUN it there. Run at &0E00, line 1 is false and line 2 clears the variables and writes REM's token (244) over line 1's IF at &0E04, so that line 1 no longer runs.

Lines 3-4, two REMs nothing runs: `(C) 4MAT 1984` and `MIKE MATSON`, each after a run of bell characters (7) and a green code (&82). LISTed, the bells sound, the two lines show in green, and the code 21 at the end of line 4 (VDU 21) turns the screen output off, so a LIST shows nothing after it.

Lines 5-6. VDU 28,0,0,0,0 shrinks the text window to the one character in the top left corner, *FX138,0,128 puts the code of function key f0 (128) in the keyboard buffer, and STOP returns to BASIC's prompt. The prompt reads f0, which the program N1 defined as `DELETE1,6|M32220|M32225|MMODE7|MRUN|M`: typed unseen in that one-character window, it deletes these first six lines and lines 32220 and 32225, selects Mode 7 and RUNs the program at &0E00.
Line 35: ON ERROR A%=0:RUN. Any error, the ESCAPE that SHIFT-f0 gives included, starts the adventure again from the beginning, A% being 0.

Lines 42-45, the program's strings: the rows of the factory's red brick walls (wa$ to wd$) and of its green double gates (g1$ to g4$), in teletext graphics, the forest's `corner of forest.` and `edge of forest.`, `It is FORBIDDEN` (bd$), `You must go back.` (mg$), six solid blocks (bl$) and twelve (s1$), `Crystal` with each letter in another colour (cr$), the Desert's soil tester words, `There is something strange here!` (sr$), `There is nothing here.` (no$), `What will you do?` (wi$), a flashing white dashed line (li$), `First you must go to the ` (A1$), `Your mission fails.` (Ym$), and the characters each kind of answer may use: Y$ `YESyesNOno`, P$ `12`, Z$ a space and the letters, J$ `NSEW`; N$, the digits, is set and never used.

Line 55. DIM e% 11, twelve bytes, of which e%?1 to e%?11 hold the eleven items of equipment (1 warm coat, 2 raincoat, 3 drink, 4 water tester, 5 metal detector, 6 soil tester, 7 fertiliser tester, 8 fright stick, 9 radio, 10 bubble-gum, 11 disguise kit; 1 = carried); b% and c% for Fibber's five instructions (asked, and which answer is right); q$, c1$ and c2$ for their words; l$(0-7) the eight places, with x% and y% their positions on the map, read from line 20000; h% for the hazards chosen on one journey; H$(1-9) the names H1 to H9 of the hazards' pictures; a$(0-41) the map's rows. Then VDU 23 turns the cursor off, VDU 26, 12 and 15 restore the windows, clear the screen and end paged mode, and *FX11,0 turns off the keys' auto-repeat. The DIM's bytes are never cleared: each RUN puts e% at the same address, so the equipment survives the RUN that ends every journey.

Line 100. The map's 42 rows are built from the DATA at line 5140: a row marked 0 is one string; a row marked 1 is a string, a run of s copies of one character, and a last string, so that the runs of spaces and blocks are stored as a count. If A% is 0, a fresh start, the progress kept in the integer variables, which RUN leaves, is set to 0: I% (lie detector), P% and N% (where the player is and is going), G% (gold pot), W% (special water), F% (fertiliser), B% (bag of soil), C% (city pass) and K% (sand goggles).
Line 120: REPEAT PROCds UNTIL FALSE. PROCds never returns, because every journey ends with RUN.

FNi(l,a%,in$,h,x,y,q), lines 240-360, every answer the player types. Line 240 draws the field: PROCv's two magenta lines above and below it, and the colour code q+128 before it, on both rows when h is 1 (double height). Line 250 turns off auto-repeat; line 270 prints l dots and empties the keyboard buffer. Line 280 waits for a key; RETURN gives back what was typed, when something was. DELETE removes the last character and puts its dot back (line 300). Line 320 makes a letter lower case, or upper case at the start of each word when a% is 3. Line 350 beeps (VDU 7) at a character not in in$ or one too many, a RETURN with nothing typed included; line 360 prints the character on each row of the field and adds it to u$, which the callers also read.

PROCe, line 400, the choice of equipment: PROCc(11) puts everything down, then PROCT offers one of the warm coat, raincoat and drink (yellow), one of the four testers (cyan), and two of the fright stick, radio, bubble-gum and disguise kit (white).

PROCT(nm$,ln,fr,to,cl), lines 430-438: one screen of the equipment. `You may take one of these items:-` in magenta on a white band, `one` or `two` flashing, a magenta box, and the items fr to to read from line ln, in colour cl. The player types an item (FNi, lower case); the first two letters are enough. An item not yet taken is marked in e% and `taken` is printed under it, with a two-second wait; anything else asks again. For `two`, `one more` flashes and the question is asked once more.
PROCc(it), line 460: clears e%?1 to e%?it, putting down the equipment. Called with 11, everything.

PROCds, lines 470-485, one stay at a place. P%=N%: the player is now where the last journey went. At the Centre (P%=0) GOSUB 550 runs its screens and A% becomes 1. Then, until a place is chosen: `You are at the:-` and the place in double height, `Where do you wish to go next ?` and the other seven places in cyan; a white box says to type Map or Carry. The answer is cut to its first two letters (FNi, capitalised). Map shows the map (PROCmap), Carry the belongings (PROCg), and both GOTO 480, the line of the REPEAT, which enters the REPEAT again without leaving the one already open: BASIC holds 20, and the 19th Map or Carry at one place stops with `Too many REPEATs`, which ON ERROR turns into a fresh start (live).

Lines 500-522. N% becomes the place whose first two letters were typed, or 10 for none. The player's own place gets `You are already there.`; `River` gets `Sorry` and `Permission is not granted`; `Danger Area` gets `It is FORBIDDEN.` flashing; both then, like anything else unknown, get `Please try again.` (N%=10).

Lines 528-546. When N% is a different place, the travel permit: `Government of Crystal`, `TRAVEL PERMIT` in white on blue, `Issued by Jim`, `TRAVELLING FROM:-` and `TRAVELLING TO:-` with the places, and `Are these details correct?`. No goes back to the question. Then PROCp, the path, whose No also goes back; PROChaz, the hazards; and the place's own function, called by name: EVAL("FN"+l$(N%)) runs FNCentre, FNCity and so on. Line 546 RUNs the program again, which ends the journey: the player is at N%.

Lines 550-570, GOSUBed by PROCds at the Centre. On a fresh start (A%=0): `To begin press`, Super Jim (PROCj), `This is Crystal Centre.` and `Your adventure begins!` flashing. Otherwise PROCk's frame and `You are at the:- Centre`. Then the treasures are counted from line 20200 and PROCend runs when all seven are held. Every arrival at the Centre gives a new weather report (PROCw), `Please choose your equipment.`, the choice (PROCe, which puts down everything carried first) and the map.

PROCp, lines 600-650, the way between P% and N%, decided by FNl, the distance between them. Forest to Desert (6) and Forest to Mountains (7) fall in the river (PROCriv). City and Forest, 10 apart, send the player to the Hills first (`First you must go to the Hills`, N%=5); a distance of 9, the Centre and the Forest, to the Factory (N%=2). A distance of 3, 4 or 6, of 10 between City and Lake, or of 5 between places whose numbers add up to an even number has a path (line 700). Anything else has none (line 710).
Line 700: `You follow the path.`; one hazard follows (PROChaz).

Line 710: `There is no path to follow.`, `The journey could be dangerous.` and `Are you sure that you want to go this way?`; hz=TRUE makes PROChaz choose two hazards, and No goes back to the question at line 480.
PROCriv, line 800: `You fall in the river and have to be rescued.`, Super Jim (PROCj), and PROCf(0) takes the player back to the Centre.

PROCg, lines 900-920, Carry: `You are carrying:-`, then on the left in yellow each item of equipment whose byte in e% is 1, and on the right in green each treasure held. The treasures come from line 20200, whose DATA gives each one's integer variable by name: READ evaluates a numeric item as an expression, so READ W gets I%, K% and the rest.

PROChaz, lines 1000-1050: one hazard on a journey, two when there is no path (hz). Each is a number 1 to 9 chosen at random, never twice on one journey: 1 green fog, 2 rain, 3 snow, 4 sun, 5 Fright Freak, 6 Blids, 7 Pouncer, 8 Grubble's Grabbers, 9 a scene. Snow is chosen again unless the weather report gave snow (H%), rain unless it gave rain (R%), and sun unless it gave sun (M%). 9 runs PROCh9, the others PROChz.

PROChz, lines 2000-2100, hazard H: its picture, by name (EVAL of FNH1 to FNH8), then its record from the DATA at line 3020, read H times: two lines of warning in red on a white band, two choices, and the line numbers of their outcomes. `You may:-`, `1.` and `2.` in a white box; the answer is 1 or 2 (FNi). The screen is cleared, each row given green or yellow text at random, and GOSUB jumps to the outcome's line number, read from the DATA.
PROCk, line 2620, the frame of the Centre's screens: flashing white dashed lines on rows 3 and 21, a red box over rows 6-18, PROCsq's coloured squares, and a text window inside the box.

PROCB(a,b,s,ln,c), lines 2630-2632: a box of teletext graphics from row a to row b, its left edge at column s and its inside ln wide, in graphics colour c, with rounded corners; the menu's procedure, the same in every program of the disc.
PROCsq, line 2650: twice, a burst of sound (PROCsound) and then nine squares, two characters tall, along each of rows 1, 4, 19 and 22, each in a colour chosen at random.

PROCw, lines 2720-2790, the weather report. CALL &AD0 prints `WEATHER REPORT`; one of six forecasts is read from line 20100: `Today will be warm and dry.`, `very cold.` or `wet and windy.`, or `High temperatures`, `Snow showers` or `Heavy rain can be expected.` The first and fourth set M% (sun), the second and fifth H% (snow), the third and sixth R% (rain), and clear the other two, which PROChaz reads.

PROCf(N%), line 2800, the end of a journey that goes somewhere else: the parameter is N% itself, the place where the player will be, and RUN starts the program again before the procedure ends, so N% keeps the new value. N%=10 means the mission has failed: A%=0 and RUN start the adventure from the beginning.

Lines 3020-3026, hazard 1. `There is a green fog all around you.` Keep going: half the time the player is lost and finds themselves at a place chosen at random. Call Super Jim: with the radio he comes to the rescue and the journey goes on; without it, as keeping going.
Lines 3030-3036, hazard 2. `It is starting to rain.` Carrying on is safe with the raincoat; without it, or going back, the player returns to where the journey began (PROCf(P%)).

Lines 3040-3046, hazard 3. `It has started to snow.` Keeping going needs the warm coat, or the player goes back. Going back: one time in four (RND(4)=2) they get lost and Super Jim takes them to the Centre; otherwise they struggle back to where they started.

Lines 3050-3057, hazard 4. `The sun is beginning to get hot.` A drink lets the journey go on; with none, Super Jim's rescue to the Centre (line 3055). Keeping on going: one time in four the player's tongue swells and Jim rescues them; otherwise they find an ice-cream stall and go on.

Lines 3060-3066, hazard 5. `It is night and a Fright Freak is standing right in front of you.` Leaving your belongings and running: the journey goes on, but every item of equipment is lost (PROCc(11)), though the message says some, and with a fright stick `You should have used your fright stick.` Hoping: the fright stick protects; without it, one time in four the Freak's picture (FN10), `That's the end of you!` and a fresh start (PROCf(10)); otherwise safety.

Lines 3070-3076, hazard 6. `The Blids are beneath you.` Bubble-gum gets the player away, and is used up; without it, fighting. Fighting: one time in four the Blids capture them, `Your mission fails.` and a fresh start; otherwise the Blids `wriggle away feeling very silly.`

Lines 3080-3086, hazard 7. `It sounds like a Pouncer is coming.` Both answers show the Pouncer (FN11). Hiding in the bushes is safe one time in four (RND(4)=1); the other three, `You have been pounced on.` and a fresh start. Telling it to go away is never fatal: one time in four it takes all the equipment (line 3092), though it says some, otherwise it leaves the player alone.

Lines 3090-3096, hazard 8, and line 3092, which the Pouncer uses too: `You will have to continue without them.` and all the equipment lost. `Grubble's Grabbers are chasing you.` Fighting loses all the equipment one time in four (`Some of your belongings are stolen.`), and wins otherwise; the disguise kit makes them leave; without one, a fight.

PROCh9, line 3100, hazard 9, which does nothing to the player: one of four scenes chosen at random by name, FN10 to FN13 (the Fright Freak, the Pouncer, the earth shaking, voices singing `We love Grubble`), then its sentence from line 20050 in green or yellow, double height.

PROCmap, lines 5060-5070, the map, `a Super Jim special`. *FX4,1 makes the arrow keys give codes (136-139) instead of editing, *FX11,25 turns auto-repeat back on, after a quarter of a second, the instructions are printed on rows 17-24, and PROCq scrolls the map in a window of rows 0-16.

PROCq, lines 5090-5105: prints the map's rows 0-15, then waits for keys. Up arrow (139) prints the next row at the bottom of the window, which scrolls the map up to show the south, as far as row 41; down arrow (138) moves the cursor up from the top of the window, which scrolls it down, and prints the row above. Each step sounds a note whose pitch falls as the map goes south. RETURN ends it and *FX4,0 gives the arrow keys back to editing.

Lines 5140-5170, DATA, rows 0-29 of the map (line 100): on a white ground: `DANGER AREA` in a red frame at the top, a row of magenta mountains, the Desert in yellow, the Lake, the Forest and its trees, and the Hills, with dotted magenta paths.

Lines 5180-5200, DATA, rows 30-41 of the map: the Hills in green, the Factory in black and yellow, the City's red buildings on yellow, and the Centre in a blue box on cyan, joined by dotted magenta paths.
FNCentre, line 10000, which returns at once: the Centre's screens are run by PROCds when the next RUN arrives there.

FNCity, lines 10500-10510, the City of Ruins: its background (PROCF), a magenta column, and the four pieces of machine code that draw a ruined building in front of the city in magenta with green cracks, &900 (which runs on into &994), &994 again, &C00 and &C93.

Lines 10630-10646. The foot of the ruin is printed, and a piece of it falls from the top, row by row down column 4, with a falling note (SOUND with pitch 1020/W), to land as a heap with a crash (SOUND on the noise channel). Then the city again, and `You have a pass to enter the city.`, or `It is FORBIDDEN to enter the city.` and back to the place's menu.

Lines 10647-10650: `Which building will you enter?` Green, Red, Yellow or Blue, by the first two letters. Green: `The ceiling has just collapsed on your head.`; Red: a Blid nest, where the player tells the little Blids stories; both set A%=0, so that the RUN after them is a fresh start. Yellow goes to line 10700, Blue to line 10720; any other answer asks again.

PROCF, line 10660, the City's background: `CITY OF RUINS` in red on row 0, a blue sky over rows 1-6, a white edge down the right, and four buildings in green, red, yellow and cyan (PROCH); the cyan one is the `Blue` building.
PROCH(x,y,c), line 10670: one building of the City, five rows tall from row y at column x, in graphics colour c, with windows.
Line 10700, the yellow building: `There is something strange here! It looks like a lie detector. You take it with you.` (I%=1), or `There is nothing here.` once it is held.

Lines 10720-10730, the blue building: `Here are sacks of fertiliser.` With the fertiliser tester (e%?7), `Using your tester you find the right sack.` (F%=1); without it, `You cannot find the right sack.` Once found, `There is nothing here.`

FNFactory, lines 11000-11131, Grubble's bubble gum factory, drawn in BASIC: a cyan sign on two posts, green double gates between red brick walls, `GRUBBLE'S BUBBLES` flashing in magenta, three chimneys (PROCi), and a lorry driven across from column 6 to 36 (PROCl), with a sound as it starts and halfway.

Lines 11135-11160. With the city pass already held, `The gate is locked.` and the journey ends. Otherwise `Are you going in the factory?`: No continues on the way; yes with the disguise kit goes to line 11190; yes without it, `You are caught, blindfolded, and taken to another part of Crystal`, a place chosen at random (PROCf).

Lines 11190-11191: `Wearing your disguise kit you enter the factory dressed as one of Grubble's workers.` The player finds a card, `SPECIAL PASS`, `This pass will permit you to enter the City.`, and takes it (C%=1).
PROCi(a,p,q), line 11210: one of the factory's chimneys, seven rows from row a at column p in graphics colour q, with a pattern of bricks at its foot.
PROCl(x,y), lines 11220-11240: the lorry at column x of row y, its cab alone near the left, then with its trailer of red separated graphics, its wheels a row of O's; at columns 20 and 36 it pauses.

FNForest, lines 11500-11515, Grubble's gum forest, a grid 8 squares wide (g%, 0 west to 7 east) and 7 deep (h%, 0 north to 6 south). The player starts at the edge facing where they came from: from the Hills at g%=1, h%=6; from the Lake at 0, 3; from the Factory at 7, 6; otherwise anywhere. Each square draws a row of five trees and a row of four in one colour, which depends on g%+h%, and opens a text window under them.

Lines 11551-11555, what each square holds, by w%=g%*h%. A Zap Gate where w% is a multiple of 4 and g% is 1 to 3 sends the player to a place chosen at random. Workers taking gum where w% is a multiple of 5 and g% is 1 to 5, and Grubble's Grabbers near where w% is 17 to 19 or 31 to 41, are warnings alone. Where w% is a multiple of 3 and h% is 1 or 2 the player is captured and taken to a square chosen at random. At g%=2, h%=1, `There is something strange here!` four times, the gold pot (line 11700), and the player leaves the forest (PROCf(3)).

Lines 11558-11650: the location (line 11900), `Which direction? (N/S/E/W)`, and one step, unless it would leave the grid. The loop's flag, of, is set FALSE and never TRUE, so the only ways out are the gold pot's square and a Zap Gate.

Lines 11700-11702: `There is an empty hole in the ground.` once G% is set; with the metal detector, `you find a gold pot hidden in the soil` (G%=1); without it, `You need a metal detector to find it`.
PROCt1(a,b), line 11830: one of the forest's back trees, the row of five along the top of the screen, four rows from row b at column a, its crown in the square's colour (CHR$w) and its trunk in blue.
PROCt2(a,b), line 11840: one of the forest's front trees, the row of four under the back row, five rows, its crown in the square's colour and its trunk in blue.

Lines 11900-11940, `Location`: a corner's name (`NORTH-WEST corner of forest.` and the others, from line 20060), or the edge the player is on, and `g% km from west edge of forest` and `6-h% km from south edge of forest`; in a corner the distances are left out.

FNLake, lines 12000-12020, the Lake: a cyan sky, a yellow shore, green grass, three mountains (PROCm) in red, blue and magenta, the lake itself drawn by the machine code at &A81, &9BC and &A51, five red trees (PROCtr) and a row of red flowers, which the bottom three rows' CLS removes after two seconds to make room for `< S >`.

Lines 12100-12140. With the special water already held (W%), Fibber says `Not you again! Go away.` and that is all. Otherwise `You are about to meet Fibber. He will give you 6 instructions. 3 of the instructions will be the opposite of what they should be.`

Lines 12150-12160. Fibber's first instruction, always the same: `You will have to leave my lake.`, Go away or Stay. Go away ends the visit; Stay is right. Then `You switch on your lie detector.` and its box (PROCy) when I% is set, or `Oh dear. You forgot your lie detector.`

Lines 12170-12190. The five instructions of line 12280 are read and asked in an order chosen at random, each once, until all five are answered or one is wrong (fib). All right: `Clever you! You've beaten me.`, and with the water tester (e%?4) the special water is found (W%=1); without it, `But you won't be able to find the special water in the lake.`

Lines 12200-12250: one instruction in Fibber's box, the lie detector's answer to `TRUTH?` (NO when c%?v is 1, the instruction a lie; YES when 2) if I% is set, and the choice (PROCch). Choice 2 is right for a lie and choice 1 for the truth: `Correct choice`, or `Caught you out! That was a fib! Now you won't be able to stay.`
PROCa, line 12260: Fibber's red box and `Fibber of the Lake says:-` in white on red.
PROCch(c1$,c2$), line 12270: a yellow box with `What will you do?`, `1.` c1$ and `2.` c2$; a$ is the answer, 1 or 2.
PROCtr(a,b), line 12272: one of the Lake's trees, a round red crown three rows tall and a white trunk.

PROCm(x,y,d), lines 12274-12276: a mountain eight rows tall from row y, its peak at column x and two columns wider each row, in graphics colour 145+d; each row's two edge characters are one of four slopes chosen at random, so no two mountains are alike.

Lines 12280-12290, DATA: Fibber's five instructions, each with 1 (a lie) or 2 (true) and its two choices: `Go into the cave on the left.` (1), `Walk forwards through the mist.` (1), `Go up the mossy, stone steps.` (1), `Go under the old wooden fence.` (2) and `Look behind Silver Sky Hill.` (2). With the first, four of his six instructions are lies, though he says three.
PROCy, line 12300: the lie detector's cyan box, `LIE DETECTOR` and `TRUTH?`.

FNHills, lines 12500-12550, the `HILLTOP SWAPSHOP`: `Today's Special Offer`, `Exchange your old radio for a pair of sand goggles`, or the other way round when the goggles are held (K%). `Are you interested?` No ends the visit; with neither, `You don't have a radio to swap.` Otherwise `You now own a ...`: the radio's byte in e% is cleared and K% set, or the reverse. The goggles are one of the seven treasures, so swapping them back loses one.

FNDesert, lines 13000-13035: `You are about to enter the Desert.`, `WARNING` flashing, `It could be very dangerous if you go any further.` (with goggles) or `It is dangerous to proceed any further without eye goggles.`, and `Do you wish to turn back?`; an answer starting with Y ends the visit.

Lines 13040-13070, the sandstorm: a yellow screen filling with dots from the bottom row up, with sound on the noise channel, then `SANDSTORM` fifty times in random colours. With the bag of soil already held, `Luckily you survive.` Otherwise `You are buried in the sand.`: without goggles, `What a silly you are.` and Super Jim takes the player to the Centre (N%=0); with them, `You find some sacks of soil`, and the soil tester (e%?6) finds the right one (B%=1).

FNMountains, line 13500: three mountains (PROCm) in green, blue and yellow, the Bird of Doom drawn by the machine code at &CC1, `The BIRD OF DOOM is over the peaks.` and `Time to leave !` Nothing is found here.
FNH1, line 15000, the green fog's picture: rows 0-21 turned green (a green new background), then a pause of 0.6 seconds.
FNH2, line 15100, the rain's picture: white exclamation marks falling for six seconds (PROCr).
FNH3, line 15200, the snow's picture: white asterisks falling for six seconds, more slowly than the rain.
FNH4, line 15300, the sun's picture: rows 0-21 turned red.
FNH5, line 15400, the night of the Fright Freak: thirty asterisks, stars, at random places.

PROCn(f1$,f2$), line 15922: the tips of the Fright Freak's fingers, eight characters, f1$ on the left hand and f2$ on the right, printed in turn to make them twitch.
PROCE1, line 15924: the Fright Freak's eyes, slanted, on rows 6-8.

FN11, line 16000, the Pouncer: its strings (legs, feet, arms, a yellow head h1$ and h2$), its body drawn by PROCo, two leaps (PROCup), and the screen scrolled up twelve lines.
PROCo, lines 16014-16018: the Pouncer's red body, thirteen rows from row b at column a, with its yellow head on top and a blue mouth on a red band.

PROCup, lines 16020-16024, the Pouncer's leap: twice its arms are held out level and dropped again (PROCar(152), then PROCar(145)); then a crouch, its legs and feet concealed, the screen scrolled down a row (VDU 30, 11) and the feet printed again under the body; legs and feet restored, the screen scrolled up 13 lines (PROCu), taking the Pouncer off the top, and down again a line at a time; a sound; and its head brought down from the top of the screen to its body, row by row: the pounce.

PROCar(z), lines 16026-16028: the Pouncer's arms. Line 16026 prints the hanging arms, four rows on each side, each row after the code z; line 16028 then, with z=152 (conceal), prints the arms held out level along row b+8 (ar$, am$), so 152 swaps the hanging arms for the level ones; with 145 (red graphics) the hanging arms show and conceal codes hide the level ones.
FN12, line 16500: `THE E A R T H SHAKES !` and `THE G R O U N D CRACKS !` in double height.
FN13, line 16700: `Voices can be heard singing:-` and `'We love Grubble'`, each letter in another colour.
PROCr(j,ki$,t), line 17000: for six seconds (TIME>600), two characters ki$ in colour j at random places along row 0, a wait of t*10 seconds, and a reverse scroll (VDU 30, 11), so that they fall.

PROCj(sp), lines 17500-17511, Super Jim: after `< S >`, the screen clears and Jim slides from column 4 to 12, drawn in teletext graphics: yellow hair, a white face with glasses and a red smile, a green jumper, cyan trousers and red boots. With sp=1, `< S >` again after.

PROCend, lines 19000-19037, the end of part 1: `The moment you've been waiting for!`, Super Jim, `CONGRATULATIONS` thirty times down the diagonal in random colours, then in a yellow box `You have completed the first part of your task. Don't forget!` Then `Part 2 is a separate program.`, `Press key F to finish.` and `Press key S to start again.` S starts a fresh game; F prints `END` and asks again, so S is the only way on.

Lines 32220-32225, run once at &1900. *TAPE selects the cassette filing system, so the disc's filing system, whose workspace is about to be written over, is no longer in use. The program is copied to &0E00 four bytes at a time (I%!&E00=I%!PAGE), TOP's high byte (&13) is lowered by the 11 pages moved, PAGE is set to &0E00, and RUN starts the copy, 2,816 bytes lower.
The end of the program, &0D and &DD. BASIC II writes &0D &FF, but any byte from &80 up after a &0D ends a program, since it cannot be a line number's high byte.
